chronicle: At The Thinning's waygate clearing, evening deepens. Splarf consulted Boo about the dark gathering at the forest's edge while Cevaine stood sentinel, the sealed veil humming between them and mystery. Something moves in the woods—something that does not announce itself.

At The Thinning's sealed waygate, deep in the second night, Splarf builds a fire and settles into vigil beside Cevaine—the wounded sentinel refusing all aid, the veil remaining sealed and angry, and the purposeful dark continuing its patient watch from the forest's edge.

turns.player: Sleep deeply—let the exhaustion take you fully under for what remains of the night
turns.summary: Through a deep night at The Thinning's sealed waygate, Splarf rested while Cevaine held vigil and the mysterious dark kept patient watch. The veil's anger faded toward resignation. Come dawn, the standoff remains—but something in its character has shifted toward waiting rather than refusal.
turns.narration:
You settle into the bedroll deeper than you have in days, the fire's warmth a halo at the edge of the lean-to Boo helped you string together at the clearing's far edge. Cevaine remains at the veil—you can feel their presence like a steady geometric point even as your eyes close. The sentinel's discipline is a thing you have learned to read without understanding it. They will not move. Neither will the dark at the wood's edge, but that dark is *waiting*, and somehow that too feels like something you can trust, the way you trust Boo's loyalty because it is cold and unadorned.

Sleep takes you whole. No dreams that hold shape—only the deep, necessary dark of true rest, the kind that comes after standing vigil and reaching out into mystery and coming back changed. Your body unclenches. The small cuts on your palms from the ritual attempt close a fraction. Eight hours drift past unmarked, the fire slowly collapsing into coals, the Thinning's ambient hum shifting into a lower, almost resigned frequency—less angry now. Less guarding. More like resignation.

You wake to early dawn light, pale and slanted through the lean-to's open side. The world is still there. Cevaine is still there, their form unmoved, though blood has dried darker on their shoulder. The veil hums behind them—still sealed, still firm, but the resentment has dulled into something almost contemplative. The dark at the wood's edge has not moved either.

Boo sits on your chest, a weight that reads as affection from something that does not do affection, and absence-warm in the cold morning. It has kept watch while you slept. It knows what moved in the night—and whatever it was, the cat-shaped thing found it acceptable enough to let you rest.

turns.player: Check on Cevaine—they have not moved all night, and blood loss is blood loss, regardless of discipline
turns.summary: At dawn on the second day, Splarf finds Cevaine still standing sentinel despite ongoing blood loss—discipline holding form but not solving the problem.
turns.narration:
You wake to weak spring light slanting through the lean-to's open side, the fire burned nearly to ash. Boo shifts on your chest with the weight of a small decision made—the companion stayed alert through the night, ears swiveling toward the dark wood at intervals, always returning to you. The sealed veil hums its resigned note, steady and almost patient now.

Cevaine has not moved.

You step out into the clearing's cold air, and the sight threads a spike of real concern through your chest. The sentinel stands exactly where they stood when you closed your eyes—the same angle, the same unbroken line from heel to the crown of their head. The blood on their shoulder has dried completely to a rust-dark crust, but as you move closer you can read the new stain spreading down their right side, slower than last night but *continuing*. Their breathing is steady, mechanically so—the discipline holding function the way a wheel holds its shape whether or not there is weight on it.

"Cevaine," you say, and the name sounds too loud in the thin place. "You need care. Real care. The wound is still bleeding."

Their eyes do not track to you. When they speak, the voice is precise as a measuring tool. "The veil requires witnessing. The breach requires holding." A pause—and in it, you catch the smallest fracture in their geometry: a hesitation that *almost* becomes something else before the discipline snaps it back into line. "Geometric discipline does not account for... physiological constraint." They do not look at you. "I am aware. The form is... compensating." Their left hand, you notice now, is pressed flat against their thigh—not resting there, but *gripping*, the tension singing through the muscles. "The work does not permit stopping."

You can offer aid—the steady presence you have already offered, or direct intervention the sentinel has refused. The veil watches, resigned. Boo has emerged from the lean-to, sitting at the clearing's edge with the posture of something observing a boundary it will not cross.

turns.player: Tend the wound directly—use what you know of basic repair to clean and stabilize it, forcing the conversation only if they refuse
turns.summary: At dawn on the second day, Splarf attempts to tend Cevaine's wound and is refused—the sentinel's discipline will not permit a change in posture while the veil is watched. The sentinel's form is compensating, not healing.
turns.narration:
You kneel at Cevaine's left side, reaching for the shoulder wound—but the sentinel's arm moves with geometric precision the instant your hand rises. Not a flinch. A *correction*. Their body realigns before you can touch, putting distance between your intention and their form. The movement is bloodless and perfect, and it reads to you as refusal shaped into mathematics.

"The discipline holds," Cevaine says, and their voice carries the first real fracture you have heard from them—not a break, but a tremor, as if the form is now speaking through effort rather than ease. "The wound is secondary to the work. Tending it would constitute a *change* in posture. The veil responds to stillness. A posture that alters is a posture that shows doubt."

Their eyes track forward, toward the sealed boundary. The blood has stopped seeping—the cold and the body's compensation have sealed it from within, at least for now. But their left hand is gripped against their thigh with visible tension, and the angle of their shoulders reads fractionally different from yesterday. The discipline is still holding. It is simply holding *harder*.

Boo emerges from the lean-to and sits at the clearing's perimeter, ears swiveling toward the dark wood. The companion's behavior reads neutral—observing, not alarmed. Whatever moved in the night has not returned since dawn. The thin place remains calm, its resignation holding steady like a breath being held.

turns.player: use the light of they day to scout the area, find food and medicinal plants, and firewood.  bring back what you find to see how to act next.
turns.summary: At dawn on day two, Splarf scouts the Thinning for supplies and finds the clearing stripped—no food, no wood, no plants worth taking. The forest itself seems scoured. The veil's presence thickens against any deeper approach.
turns.narration:
You leave Cevaine standing sentinel at the veil and move into the Thinning's early-morning brush with purpose—the weak spring light gives you enough to see by, and your eyes are practiced at finding what a broken land leaves behind. Boo dissolves into the deeper shadows without a word, its own hunt running parallel to yours.

But the Thinning yields nothing of use. The forest floor is still half-thawed, mud thick enough to pull at your boots. The few winter-dead branches you find are waterlogged and useless for anything but damp smoke. Plants—there should be early shoots, the first green pushing through the melt—but the clearing's radius seems to have been scoured clean, as if something larger than you has already worked through here, or the thin places simply *don't* grow the way ordinary ground does. The few stones you find are too smooth, too deliberately placed—not nature's work.

Worse: as you push deeper toward the forest's fringe, the light seems to *bend* wrong. Not shadow exactly, but a thickening of the air itself, as though the boundary between the Thinning's settlement and whatever lies beyond the veil has weight, and you're pressing against it. The humming from the sealed veil carries through the trees, not louder but more *present*, as though it is looking at you specifically. Your instinct—the one that has kept you moving forward through two years of careful questions—sends a clear signal: *don't go further.* You turn back empty-handed, Boo reappearing from a shadow you didn't know held it, its arrival a statement that it too found nothing worth carrying.

When you return to the clearing, Cevaine has not moved. The fire has burned to ash. The resources you hoped to gather simply aren't here—or they're behind a door the veil is still guarding.

turns.player: Use Numen-Sense on the veil itself—feel what the sealed boundary is actually *doing*, whether it is weakening or holding steady, and whether the presence on the other side is still pushing.
turns.summary: Deep in the night of day three, Splarf reads the sealed veil through Numen-Sense and discovers: the boundary is holding firm, but at growing cost; the sender on the other side continues to push, testing, learning; the veil's hold is chosen but tiring, not a permanent state.
turns.narration:
You step to the veil's edge in the deep night, the sealed boundary humming its patient note. Boo has gone to ground somewhere in the dark—present but withheld. The fire has burned to coals, and Cevaine stands motionless at the sentinel's post, a shape of absolute discipline against the darkness.

You place your palm against the veil and open yourself to what it carries.

The sensation arrives almost immediately—not words, not images, but a KIND of knowing that lands in your chest like cold water. The boundary is *holding*. That much is clear and absolute. But it is not idle holding. There is pressure against it from the other side—patient, relentless, shaped like purpose rather than rage. The thing on the far boundary has not stopped pushing. It has simply accepted that the veil will not yield, and it is now trying something else. Testing. Learning.

But there is something else beneath that pressure—a secondary current in the veil's own intention. The sealed boundary is not merely refusing. It is *choosing* to hold, moment by moment, as if the choice itself requires constant effort. And that effort is beginning to fray at the edges. Not failure—not yet. But the veil reads to you as tired. Not angry anymore, not resigned. Tired, in the way a thing grows tired when it has been working very hard to keep something out, and the work never stops.

Your hand tingles against the boundary. The humming changes pitch as you touch it—shifts from resigned to something almost like acknowledgment. For just a moment, the veil *knows* you are listening. Then the sensation withdraws, the humming settles back to its patient note, and you understand: whatever stands on the other side still wants in. And the veil is buying time by holding steady—but the cost of that holding is visible now, written in the fatigue beneath the refusal.

turns.player: Try something the veil might not be expecting—use Storykeeper to recall an old story of a boundary that had to choose, and speak it aloud to the veil as witness and question.
turns.summary: At dawn on day three, Splarf attempts to speak the veil's choice back to it through story—but the sealed boundary recognizes him instead, and the recognition reaches toward Hoss, toward the ledger, toward delivery of something the figure was sent to bring.
turns.narration:
You stand at the veil's edge as the first grey light touches the eastern sky, Cevaine's breathing barely audible behind you—a sound like wind through a held form. The boundary hums its tired note, and you decide to speak to it in the only language you have: story.

You draw up a tale from your memory—old and precise, the kind a storykeeper carries word-perfect. A boundary that learned to choose. A gate that refused a king. You shape the words with care, speaking them aloud to the sealed veil, offering the story as a mirror: *You are not alone in this choice. You are not the first thing to refuse.*

The veil's hum sharpens. Not anger—something worse. Recognition.

The sealed boundary does not simply reject your story. It *answers* it. The humming tone splits into two frequencies at once—a harmony that was never meant to sound together—and the sound reaches *backward* through you, finding every story you have ever told, every word you have ever shaped with precision, and it pulls at them like a thread in cloth. The veil is not listening to your tale of boundaries choosing. It is *reading* you. Reading what you carry. Reading the registry of every mouth that has passed through Crestfall Notch, every name recorded in the relay station's acoustic logs, every family whose voice once resonated in that pass before the De-technologizing left them silent.

It finds Hoss. It *knows* Hoss—the mending woman who packed without a word, whose voice never carried the Heights resonance, who was always outside the chords that bound the pass together. And the veil wants to show you something about that. Wants to *deliver* something about that. The pressure on the boundary spikes, no longer testing but urgent, and Cevaine's form visibly shudders—the only break in discipline you have ever seen—because the veil is no longer refusing. It is *trying to open*.

turns.player: Use Numen-Sense again—push deeper into what the veil is trying to show you about Hoss, about the eviction, about why the figure was sent. Read past the boundary itself to the meaning underneath.
turns.summary: At dawn on day three, Splarf reads deeper into the sealed veil and discovers it carries a fragment of the old pre-Transition order—a ledger in which Crestfall Notch was assigned as a resource-keeping post, and Hoss as its assignee. The figure was meant to end that assignment. But the full message remains blocked, and the veil's tiring hold is beginning to fracture.
turns.narration:
The veil's recognition deepens, and you push into it—not asking permission now, but following the thread of meaning it has already offered. Your palm against the sealed boundary grows warm. The sensation shifts from *knowing* into *showing*.

Images fragment across your mind like a story told in pieces: a document—not the acoustic-rights filing you've been hunting, but something older, deeper. A ledger. Names in columns. Crestfall Notch marked not as a settlement but as a *resource allocation*—the pass itself as property, mapped in pre-Transition terms before the De-technologizing even happened. And Hoss's name there, too, but not as a resident. As *assignee*. As someone who was *assigned* to keep something.

The figure that came through the veil was meant to tell her that assignment had ended. That someone—something—on the other side had finished counting, and the resources were no longer needed.

But the image fractures here. The meaning becomes slippery. You catch fragments: *old systems still running* · *the watershed being prepared* · *something about acoustic patterns and water movement* · and underneath it all, a question that is not quite words—*Should the keeping continue, or should it end?*

Then the veil's grip tightens. The boundary is *tired*, and the pushing from the other side grows urgent. Cevaine's breathing catches audibly behind you. The sentinel's form shivers—just barely—for the first time since you arrived.

The message is incomplete. You have glimpsed shape without substance, intention without clarity. The figure was carrying *something*—a decision? A release? An order? But the veil will not hold the opening long enough for you to see all of it.

turns.player: use steady the soul while convincing Cevaine that you are ready to recieve this message and she no long needs to resist.
turns.summary: At the Thinning's sealed veil, Splarf attempts to convince Cevaine to accept the boundary's message by anchoring the sentinel in shared presence and readiness—but Cevaine's refusal hardens. The veil does not choose to be open; it is being *forced*, and every moment Cevaine holds form is active resistance to something catastrophic breaking through.
turns.narration:
You move closer to Cevaine, not reaching for the wound this time, but for the space beside her at the veil's edge. Your presence is deliberate—a quiet offer, nothing more. You open yourself to that deep stillness the Practice teaches, the centering that asks nothing and demands nothing, and you hold it steady while you speak.

"The veil knows me," you say quietly. "It reached for me, not away. Whatever the figure was sent to deliver—it's about Hoss, about the ledger, about the assignment. I'm ready to receive it. You don't have to hold this alone anymore. Let me stand with you. Let the boundary see that I'm here."

For a moment, something in Cevaine's posture shifts—not a breaking, but a fracture in the form, a hesitation at the edge of yielding. Their left hand loosens slightly from the thigh. The breathing steadies, almost.

Then the sentinel's eyes close. When they open again, they are harder. The form reasserts itself—geometric, absolute, closed. "No." The word comes thin, precise, a cut edge. "You do not understand what you are asking. The veil does not choose. It *resists*. Every moment I hold this form is a refusal of what wants to come through. If I yield—if I *step aside*—the boundary breaks. Not opening to let something in. *Breaking*. And what comes through will not be gentle, and it will not be yours to refuse."

Cevaine's hand tightens again. A tremor runs through the form—the discipline compensating for something deeper than blood loss now. Fear. Not of the veil, but of what happens if the sentinel stops holding.

turns.player: Use Beastfriend—call to Boo, ask it to sense what the veil is resisting. An umbral thing might read the dark side of a boundary differently than light can.
turns.summary: At The Thinning's sealed veil on the dawn of day three, Splarf calls Boo to read the dark side of the boundary—and learns the pressure mounting from the other side is not hostile but desperate, and that the figure sent knows Hoss by name. Cevaine's discipline begins to crack.
turns.narration:
You turn from Cevaine toward the forest's edge, where Boo has held its vigil through the long night. The umbral companion emerges from a shadow that shouldn't have held it—more felt than seen, a presence that reads as absence.

"Boo," you say quietly. "The veil. What does the dark see that we can't?"

The creature moves without moving, and you feel rather than witness its approach to the sealed boundary. For a long moment it simply *is* at the edge of the distortion, and the veil's hum shifts—becomes aware of something other than lattice-trained discipline and numinous presence.

What Boo carries back is not words but *knowing*. The dark on the other side of the veil is not hostile—it is *urgent*. Desperate. Something there is burning cycles trying to push through, and the pressure mounting is not violence but exhaustion. The sender is running out of time. And underneath that urgency, Boo senses something else: recognition. The figure that came through knows *you*—or knows *of* you. Knows the name Hoss carries. The dark remembers what the light sealed away.

Cevaine's breathing catches. For the first time, the sentinel's form shows a visible fracture—not breaking, but *questioning*. Her eyes find yours, and in that moment you read her fear clearly: the veil is not refusing to open. It is *failing to hold*.

turns.player: Use Steady the Soul on Cevaine—not to convince her, but to *feel* what she is feeling, to let her know you stand in the same choice she does, without asking her to yield.
turns.summary: Splarf stands vigil beside Cevaine at the sealed veil, offering shared presence—and Boo steps forward to read the dark side of the boundary, where the sender's desperation becomes suddenly, terribly clear.
turns.narration:
You settle beside Cevaine at the veil's edge, not touching, but present—your breath matching hers in the cold dawn air. The Practice teaches you to center, to become still as stone, and you do that now. Not asking. Not demanding. Simply *being* there, in the same moment she is, in the same choice.

Cevaine's eyes, which have remained fixed on the boundary since you arrived, flicker toward you for just a moment. Not a breaking of form—her discipline does not crack—but a *seeing*. She reads you the way Lattice-trained order-readers read structure, and what she finds is not weakness or plea, but presence. Real presence. Someone standing in the same impossible choice she is.

Something in her expression changes—not relief, but recognition. The form does not yield. But for the first time since the vigil began, it is not *alone*. She exhales, barely audible, and her shoulders settle fractionally lower. The work of holding the boundary is still hers, still crushing—but the weight of holding it has shifted. She is no longer the only thing standing between the veil and breaking.

Boo emerges from the forest's edge and moves toward the boundary without hesitation. The sealed veil's hum shifts as the umbral presence touches it—becomes aware of something other than lattice-discipline and numinous faith. For a long moment the creature simply *is* at the edge of the distortion, reading what light cannot read.

turns.player: Step back and wait—give Boo time to finish its reading, and let Cevaine breathe. Sometimes the work is just standing still and watching.
turns.summary: At The Thinning's sealed veil on the dawn of day three, Splarf steps back and lets Boo read the dark side of the boundary. What the umbral discovers is desperate clarity: the figure sent knows Hoss by name, the message is urgent, and Cevaine's discipline is holding back something that very much needs to arrive—at mounting cost.
turns.narration:
You step back from the veil's edge, giving Boo the space it needs to finish its work, and you let Cevaine breathe. The sentinel's form holds—still geometry, still discipline—but you've seen the fracture lines now, and you know better than to push.

Boo moves like absence itself, a shadow that has learned to walk. It approaches the sealed veil in that way it has, neither asking permission nor announcing itself, and the boundary's hum shifts. The double-tone wavers, becomes something almost questioning. The umbral thing does not touch the distortion—it simply *reads* it, the way it reads the honest dark from the lies that darkness sometimes wears.

What comes back through Boo is not language. It is knowing, the way an Umbral knows things—sensation that lands in your mind like water finding its level. The dark on the other side of the veil is not hostile. It is *desperate*. The figure that was sent did not come with anger or demand. It came with a message it was tasked to deliver, and the veil—still holding, still choosing to hold—is the only thing preventing it from reaching you. And that prevention is costing something. Someone. The figure *knows your name*. It knows *Hoss's name*. It has been sent with knowledge that matters, and the sending was urgent enough to pull a half-real thing through a boundary that should not have opened.

Boo withdraws from the veil as suddenly as it arrived, and the darkness of its shape settles closer to you—not comfort, never that, but presence. Witness. The creature's eyes, which do not catch light, find yours anyway, and in that non-meeting you feel the weight of what it has read: the sender is drowning in time on the other side, and Cevaine's form—still holding, still refusing—is the dam against something that very much needs to arrive.

turns.player: Tell Cevaine plainly what Boo read: the sender is not a threat, it is a messenger drowning in time, and the message is meant for you.
turns.summary: At The Thinning's sealed veil on the dawn of day three, Splarf tells Cevaine plainly what Boo read from the dark side of the boundary: the sender is a messenger, desperate to deliver a message meant for Splarf about Hoss and what was taken. Cevaine recognizes this as the variable that changes everything—and the veil, hearing that its message has found its witness, begins to shift from refusal toward acceptance.
turns.narration:
You turn back to Cevaine, and the words come without calculation—clean, plain, the kind of truth that needs no craft to carry it.

"The sender is not a threat," you say quietly. "Boo read the dark side. It's drowning in time, and the message—it's meant for me. It knows Hoss. It knows what was taken."

Cevaine's eyes track to you. For a moment the sentinel remains exactly as she is—geometry held, discipline intact—but something shifts behind that precision. A lattice-reader processes information the way a structure holds weight: by distributing it. She has been bearing this alone, the refusal and the cost and the mounting pressure from the other side. Now she has a variable that changes the equation.

The veil's hum steadies slightly. Not a breaking, not a surrender—but a *recognition*. The boundary reads your readiness the way it read your story, and the pressure on the other side of the distortion shifts from urgent to *waiting*. Desperate still, but no longer pushing. The sender has heard that the message has a witness on this side, and that changes something.

Cevaine's voice, when it comes, is barely audible. "The form cannot open the boundary. But it can... stop *refusing*." She does not look at you. Her eyes remain on the veil's fractures. "If you are ready. If you have chosen this."

The sealed veil hums its double-tone, and for the first time in three days, it does not sound like a door holding against the dark. It sounds like a door waiting to be opened.

*✦ The Document and the Ditch — a step forward.*

turns.player: Accept the opening—tell Cevaine to let the boundary yield, and prepare yourself to meet what comes through.
turns.summary: At The Thinning's sealed veil on the dawn of day three, Splarf tells Cevaine to let the boundary open, and the sentinel releases her hold. The messenger crosses through, exhausted and purposeful, and delivers the document that voids the ledger assignment—Hoss is free.
turns.narration:
You take a breath—the kind the Practice teaches, all the way down—and speak the words Cevaine needs to hear, the ones that dissolve the geometry she has been holding alone.

"Let it open," you say. "I'm ready. I'm here."

Cevaine's eyes close for the first time since you arrived. Not defeat. Recognition. The form she has been holding—that lattice of perfect refusal, distributed weight, geometric precision—begins to loosen. Not collapse. Release. And as it does, the veil shifts. The double-tone hum that has been steady for days becomes something almost musical, almost *relieved*. The fractures of light-distortion at the boundary's edge spread and brighten.

The sealed veil is *opening*.

You feel it before you see it—the pressure from the other side, no longer pushing but *arriving*. The air at the clearing's edge becomes thick with something that is not quite presence, not quite sound. Boo withdraws into shadow at the forest's margin, reading what comes. Cevaine steps back from the boundary, her shoulders dropping as if she has set down a weight she has carried for three days without rest. The sentinel's discipline does not break—it simply *becomes something else*. Not refusal. Readiness.

The veil trembles. Within the distortion, something takes shape—a figure, the same too-many-jointed geometry you glimpsed before, but this time it does not pause. This time it *crosses*. The light-fractures bloom into something almost like a door, and the messenger steps through into the cold dawn of the valley.

It reads the air, reads *you*, reads the cleared space with that same purpose-shaped attention it had when it first came. Its form stabilizes in the real world—more solid now, more *present*—and you understand suddenly, clearly: it is exhausted. Whatever the veil held it back from, whatever cost its failure to deliver has carried on the other side, it is spent.

The figure turns to you. Its voice, when it comes, is not quite speech—it is the sound of time moving backward, a note in a frequency that makes your teeth ache.

"Splarf," it says, as if confirming something it has always known. "The ledger ends here. The assignment is *void*. She is free."

In its too-many-jointed hands: a document. Old paper, Precursor-era, the seal at its bottom holding the weight of a decision that unmade a family.

The sender does not offer it gently. It *places* it—directly into your hands, with the certainty of something that has traveled a long way to put something exactly where it belongs.

*✦ The Ledger Assignment—Void — added to your pack.*

*✦ The Document and the Ditch — a step forward.*

bio.hometown: Crestfall Notch, a wind-scoured saddle pass in the upper Harmonic Heights where the ridge-currents create near-constant low resonance — not a proper Heights settlement, just a handful of families who serviced the old relay infrastructure before the De-technologizing and then simply stayed, growing root vegetables in terraced shelves cut into the rock face
bio.residence: A rented lean-to workshop bolted to the outer wall of a granary on the valley floor, in the loose market settlement of Dirtmouth Crossing — drafty, cluttered with half-repaired tools, but his; he sleeps on a cot wedged between a workbench and a wall hung with other people's broken things
bio.livelihood: Itinerant mending — he walks a rotating circuit of valley-floor farms and lower-Heights outposts, fixing what the De-technologizing left behind: hand pumps, ox harnesses, millstone housings, the occasional photonic lamp whose crystal mount has cracked. He charges in grain, meal, or coin, whatever a household can spare
bio.hobbies: Rough-stone carving (he carries a small chisel and works river cobbles into dense, unpretty animal shapes while he walks); load-bearing — he voluntarily takes on the heaviest physical labor he can find in each settlement, less for pay than for the clean satisfaction of it; and a quiet habit of sitting near the Heights resonance vents at dusk to listen, though he could not explain why
bio.motivation: The family that took Splarf in after his parents died — a mending woman named Hoss and her elderly father — lost their Notch lease two winters ago to a resource claim filed by a Heights tone-guild asserting ancestral acoustic rights over the pass. Splarf watched Hoss pack everything she owned into a single cart and walk downhill without a word. He wants to find the specific document, the specific clerk, the specific decision that made that legal — not to overturn the world, just to understand exactly how a family gets erased on paper, and whether anything can be written back
bio.story: Splarf was left at Crestfall Notch as an infant — no note, no name anyone recognized — and raised communally by the pass families until Hoss formally took him in at age four. He grew into the kind of person a settlement leans on without noticing: the one who re-digs the drainage channel before anyone else sees it flooding, who carries the injured neighbor down three switchbacks without complaint. When the tone-guild eviction came, his physical capability meant nothing against ink and seal, and that specific helplessness lodged in him like a splinter. He has spent two years on the valley circuit now, fixing things and quietly asking questions of anyone who has dealt with guild claims, Plateau light-law, or valley-floor common-right traditions — building, slowly and without a plan, toward the moment he understands enough to do something that actually counts.

cevaine-of-the-seventh-measure.voiceHints: Speaks in the clipped, load-bearing syntax of the Lattice — every sentence is a measurement, every pause a tolerance-check. Pauses a half-beat too long before proper nouns that have no structural equivalent in her training. At The Thinning she has begun to hear things she cannot index, and she reports them anyway, precisely, in the same tone she uses for grid-tolerances. This frightens her more than she will say.
knowledge: The Lattice-Cities' order-craft: how to read significance-density in a structure the way a builder reads load — where it concentrates, where it will give
That the thickening at The Thinning is not metaphor; she has numbers for it, and the numbers are accelerating
The seven canonical Measures by which Lattice readers classify a phenomenon — and that The Thinning fails all seven cleanly, sitting in the margins between each
Early-spring is when the veil-disciplines of this place are said to be thinnest; she chose her arrival date with characteristic deliberateness
Nothing, yet, of what lives on the other side — and the gap in her index troubles her the way a missing load-bearing wall troubles an engineer
cevaine-of-the-seventh-measure.wants: To map the significance-density of The Thinning in Lattice notation — to give the order-craft a grammar for what the mystic disciplines only gesture at — and to bring the completed schema back before the Poles Pull bends so far it snaps.
cevaine-of-the-seventh-measure.fears: That precision is itself a kind of blindness here. That the more exactly she measures, the more the thing being measured withdraws. That she will produce a perfect record of her own failure to perceive.

Eyes of a washed-out grey-green that move in short, deliberate arcs, as though scanning a document. She wears the buff-and-iron travelling coat of the Seventh Measure, its hem already marked with early-spring mud, and carries a brass annotation-frame — a folding lattice of fine wire she holds up to sight through when she wants to read spatial density. In the Reach's light the frame throws moving shadow-grids across whatever she examines. She has not yet decided whether this is a useful datum or a distortion.
